0.2 What the results say

    1. A Kaplan–Meier error law works as well as knowing the right error family. On S-Misspec (log-normal errors) the semiparametric NP-KAN-
       AFT was better than B2-S Cox and the Weibull KAN-AFT in every one of the 20 fresh replicates, and indistinguishable from the correctly specified
       log-normal KAN-AFT (-0.0010 [-0.0028, +0.0007]). Its advantage is that it does not need the family to be guessed; it is not better than the right
       parametric model. On S-Sparse it stayed within the +0.005 margin of B2-S Cox (+0.0012 [-0.0007, +0.0031]).
    2. Confirming in both halves of the validation split fixed the Round-19 gap. Against B2-S trained on the whole validation set, the cross-
       confirmed anchor kept a clear S-Last gain and stayed within +0.005 on the trajectory scenario for Cox, log-normal AFT and NP-AFT alike. Round 19’s
       Cox S-Sparse bound was +0.0063 in development; on fresh seeds Round 20’s is inside the margin.
    3. It works by deciding less often. On the trajectory scenarios anchoring was confirmed in one replicate per family; with the conservative Cox
       margin (0.02, the edge of the grid) Cox anchored in only 9 and 1 of 20 S-Last / S-Sparse replicates and gave up part of its S-Last gain (it did not
       beat landmark Cox there). Always refitting would have cost on every trajectory scenario, so the confirmation step, not the refit, carries the non-
       inferiority.
    4. Protocol. Both go rules passed on the development seeds before any fresh seed was used, every job finished (no failures), and both hypotheses
       were decided by the rules registered in D150.


Part A: Round 20

R20.1 Owner instruction (D150) and fact check

        Instruction (2026-10-31). Add a non-parametric-error KAN AFT (log T = KAN(Z) + ε, ε estimated non-parametrically; Buckley–James/Kaplan–Meier
        and smoothed-Gehan objectives compared in development) next to the Cox and parametric AFT KANs; fix the Round-19 Cox S-Sparse confirmation
        gate (+0.0063 against < +0.005) by comparing against the 3-seed B2-S ensemble and confirming in both directions of the split; develop on the
        already-used seeds 4400–4619 only; run the formal evaluation on 4700–4919 only if the go rules pass; follow D111 and the pre-registration rules;
        commit locally, do not push. Later instruction (2026-11-01): “continue and send me the report pdf”.
        Fact check (docs/round20_devplan.md §1): the seed blocks were unused; the Gehan pair order in the instruction was reversed and is implemented in
        the convex Jin–Lin–Wei–Ying form; fkan_surv.py and distill_and_replace did not exist and were created; a Buckley–James KAN-AFT for static
        covariates is already published (KAN-AFT), so no novelty claim is made; the cause of the Round-19 miss (one seed-0 member, one direction) was a
        hypothesis; the go rule “S-Last mean < 0” is weaker than the formal upper-bound rule; the verifier’s flag is ALL_CHECKS_PASS.


R20.2 Methods (as implemented)

        NP-KAN-AFT. log T = μ + η(Z) + ε with η the B2-S location (D112 ensemble: lr × wd tuned on the objective’s validation loss, seeds 0–2). bj_km:
        before every epoch the Kaplan–Meier law of the training residuals is re-estimated (largest residual counted as an event) and the loss is the mean
        squared distance to the Buckley–James targets. rank_km: smoothed Gehan loss (1/n²) Σ_{i: δ=1} Σ_j τ softplus((e_j − e_i)/τ), τ = 0.05, intercept
        fixed. Prediction: S(t | Z) = S_KM(log t − η(Z)), a right-continuous step function, 1 below the smallest residual and S_KM(largest residual) above the
        largest. distill_and_replace applies the Round-16 fixed-μ distillation with a validation-loss rollback (tested; not part of the hypotheses).
        Cross-confirmed anchor. For each direction (select on h1 = val_select, confirm on h2 = val_confirm, and the reverse) the D141 two-way gate
        runs on the selection half; the anchored 3-seed ensemble and the 3-seed B2-S ensemble of that half are scored on the other half by their mean
        member held-out loss. Confirmed iff anchoring wins by more than the margin in both directions with an active channel (NP-AFT margin relative to
        |loss|). Confirmed: the h1-direction anchored ensemble fine-tuned once more on the whole validation set (the Round-19 finetune refit). Otherwise:
        the full-validation B2-S ensemble, exactly.
       Tests: R20-1 to R20-6 (tests/test_round20.py: Kaplan–Meier and Buckley–James building blocks, Gehan gradient identity and slope recovery, survival
       recovery without the error family, prediction properties, distillation and rollback, cross-confirmation logic and exact reduction, bit-identity of the
       default paths with the Round-19 code), R20-7 to R20-11 (manuscript); the Round 15–19 tests pass; a Round-19 job reproduced its record exactly (68
       values).

R20.7 Limitations

       Settings chosen on reused seeds. The NP-AFT objective and all three margins were chosen on development seeds used for the third time
       (Round-18 formal, Round-19 development, Round-20 development); the Cox margin lies at the edge of its grid.
       Cause not established. The Round-19 miss and the Round-20 pass are on different seeds; the fresh-seed test supports the cross-confirmed
       estimator, but does not show that the one-member, one-direction comparison caused the Round-19 miss.
       One error law. NP-KAN-AFT was tested under log-normal errors only; its gain over Cox and Weibull reflects their misspecification there. Its survival
       curve is not extrapolated beyond the largest training residual.
       No novelty claim (D111). The semiparametric AFT model and Buckley–James / rank estimation are classical; a Buckley–James KAN-AFT for static
       covariates is published. New here is only their use with the functional B2-S location and the anchored gate.
       One simulator, 20 replicates per scenario; no real data in Round 20. AFCM is still not validated.

Authors: [to be completed by the owner]
Status: draft manuscript of a pre-registered empirical study; no novelty claim (D111).


Abstract

Background. Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (KANs) replace the weights of a neural network by learnable univariate functions and have been adapted to
survival analysis with static covariates (Knottenbelt et al., 2025; Jose et al., 2025). Many clinical and engineering problems instead have covariates
measured repeatedly over time. A single-layer functional KAN under the Cox loss has the same model form as the additive functional Cox model (AFCM)
(Cui et al., 2021), so any contribution must be empirical.

Methods. We report a sequence of pre-registered studies. A motivating study (framing b) embedded KAN blocks in a functional autoencoder (KAN-FAE)
and compared it with a parameter-matched MLP autoencoder (MLP-FAE). The primary study (framing a) evaluated direct functional KAN survival models:
functional CoxKAN and functional KAN-AFT with time-homogeneous (B2-H), separable bivariate (B2-S) and two-layer (B2-deep) functional layers; two-
stage models on functional principal component scores or trajectory summaries (B1); and stacked landmark supermodels (B3). Comparators were a re-
implementation of AFCM, an FPCA Cox model, a two-stage mixed-effects Cox model, summary-based Cox and random survival forest models and a
landmark Cox model. A simulation study (four scenarios, 20 replicates each) had a single confirmatory test (H-R12): B2-S Cox minus AFCM in identifiable
shape error (RISE). Real-data analyses (PBC, two JM data sets, C-MAPSS) were exploratory. A second phase (Rounds 15–20) tested, on fresh simulation
seeds and with pre-registered multi-part criteria, a distillation refit for the symbolic summaries, a landmark-anchored functional model that adds the last
observed values to B2-S, a two-way gate that can fall back to B2-S, and both tools in a log-normal KAN-AFT; the last round added a semiparametric
functional KAN-AFT whose error law is estimated by Kaplan–Meier, and a confirmation of anchoring in both halves of the validation split.

Results. H-R12 was inconclusive: B2-S Cox minus AFCM V3 was +0.0065 (95% CI [−0.0506, +0.0635]; paired-t p 0.815; equivalence within ±0.05 not
shown, TOST p 0.0634), and the AFCM comparator failed its own single-fit acceptance check. Both direct functional models recovered nonlinear shapes far
better than a linear-in-scores FPCA model (B2-S minus B1-FPCA-1: −0.5566, better in 20 of 20 replicates). Substituting accepted symbolic formulas
preserved the learned shapes (S-Add RISE 0.214 before and 0.212 after substitution), whereas the customary unconstrained refit degraded them (1.604).
On the real data no functional or KAN model predicted clearly better than simple landmark baselines; every Nadeau–Bengio interval for the integrated
Brier score of B2-S Cox minus a baseline included 0. In Phase 2, a distillation refit with a fixed anchor weight, a NaN-safe fallback and a bound on formula
arguments kept all 40 refits finite and preserved the pruned shapes (H-R16a supported, S-Add RISE difference −0.0004; its validation-tuned predecessor
H-R15a had failed). A landmark-anchored model that adds the last observed values to B2-S was clearly better than B2-S Cox when risk depended on the
last values (S-Last, −0.0176) but slightly worse when it depended on the whole trajectory (S-Sparse, +0.0032), so H-R15b and H-R16b were not
supported. A two-way gate that falls back to B2-S unless anchoring wins on validation kept the S-Last gain but again missed the S-Sparse margin on fresh
seeds (upper bound +0.0053; H-R17a not supported), while for a log-normal KAN-AFT the distillation refit and a more conservative two-way gate met
every registered criterion (H-R17b supported). Deciding on held-out validation subjects whether to anchor (Round 18) met every registered criterion for
Cox and for the AFT model (H-R18a and H-R18b supported; S-Sparse bound for Cox +0.0028), although against B2-S trained on the whole validation set
the S-Sparse bound was wider; refitting the anchored model on the whole validation set did not close that gap in a development check, so no formal test
was run (Round 19). In Round 20 the semiparametric KAN-AFT was better than B2-S Cox and a Weibull KAN-AFT under log-normal errors (H-R20a
supported; −0.0135 and −0.0150) but not shown to be better than the correctly specified log-normal KAN-AFT (−0.0010), and confirming anchoring in
both halves of the validation split against three-seed B2-S ensembles met every registered criterion against B2-S trained on the whole validation set, for
Cox and both AFT models (H-R20b supported; S-Sparse bound for Cox +0.0036). Pruning selected a stable, clinically plausible set of PBC markers, and the
leading effects were stable over 100 bootstrap fits and aligned with the pre-stated clinical directions, with one exception (prothrombin index under B2-S).
In the motivating study, KAN-FAE had higher survival-curve error than MLP-FAE in the confirmatory test (H1: +0.0078, p 0.047), the two were equivalent
under reconstruction pre-training on fresh seeds (−0.0005, TOST p 0.0049), and the autoencoder’s KAN edges acted on abstract features rather than on
clinical trajectories.

Conclusions. Direct functional KAN survival models are a workable, interpretable parametrisation of the additive functional Cox model, with usable
pruning and symbolic summaries when the formulas are substituted without refitting. We found no evidence of a predictive advantage over established
methods, and placing KAN blocks inside a functional autoencoder gave neither better prediction nor readable effects. A strongly anchored refit makes the
symbolic summaries safe to refit but does not improve on substitution alone, for Cox and AFT models alike; anchoring to the last observed values helps
when they carry the risk and is hard to switch off reliably when they do not, unless the decision is confirmed on held-out data in both directions.
Estimating the AFT error law by Kaplan–Meier removes the need to choose an error family. All findings beyond the registered hypotheses (H1, H-R12, H-
R15a/b, H-R16a/b, H-R17a/b, H-R18a/b, H-R20a/b) are exploratory.


Keywords

Kolmogorov–Arnold networks; functional data; survival analysis; additive functional Cox model; landmarking; pre-registration; equivalence testing;
negative results; symbolic regression; interpretability.


1. Introduction

1.1 Functional covariates in survival analysis

Repeated measurements of a biomarker or a sensor are naturally viewed as a curve X(t) observed with noise at a few times (Ramsay & Silverman, 2005).
The linear functional Cox model enters the curve through ∫β(t)X(t)dt (Gellar et al., 2015; Kong et al., 2018), and its coefficient can also vary with follow-up
time (Du & Leroux, 2024). The additive functional Cox model (AFCM) of Cui et al. (2021) replaces the linear term by ∫F(X(s), s)ds with a bivariate smooth
F, following functional generalised additive models (McLean et al., 2014); it is estimated with penalised tensor-product splines. Sparse, irregular visits are
commonly handled by principal components analysis through conditional expectation (PACE) (Yao et al., 2005). Dynamic prediction uses joint models
(Wulfsohn & Tsiatis, 1997; Tsiatis & Davidian, 2004; Rizopoulos, 2010), landmarking and landmark supermodels (van Houwelingen, 2007; van
Houwelingen & Putter, 2012; Putter & van Houwelingen, 2022), or deep models of the covariate history (Lee et al., 2020; Hu & Nan, 2025; Gao et al.,
2025).

Neural Cox models such as DeepSurv (Katzman et al., 2018) gain flexibility at the cost of readable effects. KANs (Liu et al., 2025) place a learnable
univariate function on every edge, which makes each edge a candidate for visualisation, pruning and symbolic regression. CoxKAN (Knottenbelt et al.,
2025), KAN-AFT (Jose et al., 2025), SurvKAN (Mastroleo et al., 2026) and KAPLAN (Boulitsakis Logothetis et al., 2026) all use static covariates; their time-
varying elements concern effects that change with follow-up time, not covariates measured over time. A KAN joint model with yearly landmarks was
found only as a conference abstract (Lundin et al., 2025), and F-KAN feeds functional principal component scores to a KAN for a scalar response (Qin & Li,
2026).

1.2 Architectural motivation: KAN blocks inside a functional autoencoder

The project began (Rounds 1–9) with a different architecture: a functional autoencoder (Wu et al., 2024) whose encoder used KAN blocks, with an AFT
survival head on the latent representation (KAN-FAE), against a parameter-matched MLP encoder (MLP-FAE). The hope was that a KAN encoder would give
both better prediction and readable effects. Two findings ended that line (Section 3.7 gives the numbers).

   1. No predictive advantage. The conventional MLP-FAE first had to pass a pre-registered learnability gate; every design failed it until Round 8 (Table
      1 lists the gate looks with saved verdict records). Under the configuration that passed, the single confirmatory test (H1) found KAN-FAE worse than
      MLP-FAE in survival-curve error. With reconstruction pre-training (strategy S3) the two were indistinguishable, and a fresh-seed re-test in Round 12
      declared them equivalent within a pre-registered margin.
   2. No clinical readability. In an autoencoder the KAN edges act on abstract front-end features and feed latent units that a further head combines
      into risk. Pruning removed almost no edge, and the symbolic formulas, though accurate, described maps between abstract coordinates rather than
      effects of a clinical variable.

These results motivated the direct design studied in the rest of this paper: put the KAN where the clinical variable enters, ∫φ(X(t), t)dt, so that each
learned function is an effect of a measured trajectory.

Claim policy (D111). We make no novelty or “first” claim; that would require a systematic review including the full texts of JM-KAN, F-KAN and KAPLAN.
We claim no superiority where an interval includes 0 or where the comparator was not validated. The contributions are: (i) a pre-registered empirical
comparison of functional KAN survival models with AFCM and other functional methods; (ii) a measured evaluation of shape recovery, channel selection,
symbolic extraction, stability and clinical alignment; (iii) the negative architectural result for KAN-FAE; (iv) a reproducible benchmark in which every
number is traceable to a saved record.


2. Models and estimation

2.1 Data and notation

Subject i has D longitudinal channels X_id(t) observed with noise at times t_ij in a history window, rescaled to [0, 1], scalar covariates z_i, and a possibly
right-censored outcome (Y_i, δ_i). Curves are reconstructed on a fixed grid of 50 points, either by per-subject penalised B-spline smoothing (12 basis
functions; smoothing parameter chosen on held-out points of training subjects) or by PACE (Yao et al., 2005). Integrals are trapezoid quadratures on the
grid. Inputs to every KAN are standardised with training statistics so that each edge can be read in original units after back-transformation.

2.2 Survival losses

Cox. The linear predictor η_i has no intercept. The negative log partial likelihood (Cox, 1972) is computed exactly under the Breslow and Efron tie
corrections (Breslow, 1974; Efron, 1977) (Efron by default), and the baseline cumulative hazard is the Breslow estimator, giving S(t | x) = exp(−Λ̂₀(t)e^η).
CoxKAN’s published fast approximation of the loss is not used; this is a disclosed deviation. Acceptance tests confirmed the loss against lifelines and a
direct formula (difference below 1e-8) and the baseline against lifelines (below 1e-6).

Accelerated failure time (KAN-AFT). log T = μ + η + σε with a Weibull (Gumbel ε) likelihood. Residual calibration (b2s_aft_rc) keeps the fitted
location and scale but predicts S(t | x) = Ŝ_ε((log t − μ̂ − η̂)/σ̂), where Ŝ_ε is the Kaplan–Meier estimate (Kaplan & Meier, 1958) of the standardised
training residuals, so that the error law is not assumed.

2.3 Model families

      B1 (two-stage interpretable coordinates). B1-FPCA: functional principal component scores per channel (95% variance explained, at most 5
      components; PACE as an alternative front end in the sparse simulation), with z, feed a one-layer additive KAN (B1-FPCA-1) or a two-layer KAN [p → 4
      → 1] (B1-FPCA-2). B1-SUM: per-channel summaries (last value, mean, OLS slope, residual SD) feed the same heads.
      B2 (functional KAN layer on X(t)).
            B2-H (time-homogeneous): η = Σ_d ∫φ_d(X_d(t))dt + Σ_k ψ_k(z_k).
            B2-S (separable bivariate, rank 2): φ_d(x, t) = Σ_m g_dm(x)h_dm(t), with every g and h a univariate KAN edge; the surface is read in x and t
            separately.
            B2-deep: the functional summaries ∫g_dm(X_d(t))h_dm(t)dt feed a second KAN layer [D·M + p → 4 → 1], which can represent interactions
            between channels.
            Each φ_d is centred over the training data (the constant is absorbed by the baseline). The primary input scale is standardised X; a quantile-
            transformed input (Cui et al., 2021) is a sensitivity analysis.
      B3 (stacked landmark supermodel). For each landmark t_L and subject at risk, features from the history window before t_L only, outcome
      administratively censored at t_L + w, one row per (subject, landmark); a CoxKAN with a landmark-stratified baseline and t_L as an additional input
      edge (van Houwelingen & Putter, 2012). The linear comparator is the same supermodel with linear effects (b3_cox).

KAN layers are B-spline KANs (grid 5, order 3, SiLU base). Every KAN model is a three-member ensemble: learning rate {1e-3, 3e-3} × weight decay {1e-
4, 1e-3} tuned on the validation loss with seed 0, then seeds 0–2 trained at the chosen setting (Adam, early stopping with patience 100, at most 3,000
epochs). The ensemble’s prediction and shape estimate are the members’ means, which is valid because η is additive in φ; the seed-0 member is also
reported.

2.4 Comparators

      AFCM (Cui et al., 2021): ∫F(X(s), s)ds with F a 10 × 10 tensor-product cubic B-spline, difference penalties in x and t, penalised partial likelihood. R
      was not available, so AFCM is a Python re-implementation with smoothing parameters chosen by validation partial likelihood instead of REML in
      mgcv. V3 (the primary comparator) uses a widened λ_x grid {1e-7, …, 1e1} × λ_t {1e-4, 1e-2, 1, 1e2, 1e4}, penalties normalised by basis size and a
      first- plus second-order difference penalty in t. V0, the earlier version, is a sensitivity row. Validation caveat: V3 was chosen on one development
      seed and then failed its pre-registered single-fit acceptance check (CK-6c): on a fresh seed its identifiable RISE for the time-homogeneous effect
      was 0.247 against a threshold of 0.15. AFCM is therefore an unvalidated comparator throughout.
      fpca_cox: linear Cox on FPCA scores (the FLCRM model class (Kong et al., 2018)).
      lme2_cox: per-channel linear mixed model with random intercept and slope (Laird & Ware, 1982), fitted by EM; the BLUPs at the landmark enter a
      Cox model (a two-stage, joint-model-style baseline; JM itself was not available).
      sum_cox, sum_rsf: Cox and random survival forest (Ishwaran et al., 2008) on trajectory summaries.
      landmark_cox: Cox on the last observed values at the landmark plus z (van Houwelingen, 2007).
      static CoxKAN: CoxKAN on the last observed values plus z. flat_ae: an autoencoder on the curve values on the grid, flattened into one vector
      (sparse simulation only).
2.5 Pruning and channel selection

Training adds λ·(|Φ|₁ + 2·entropy(Φ) + |C|₁) to the loss. For channel selection the score of channel d is the mean absolute deviation of its integrated
functional effect over the training subjects, normalised by the largest channel score; a channel scoring below θ_rel loses all its functional edges, and a
pruned edge’s mean is absorbed by the baseline. The grid is λ {0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2} × θ_rel {0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25}, each point
fine-tuned for 200 epochs with the mask fixed. The selection rule is parsimonious: among grid points within 0.01 (mean negative log partial likelihood per
event) of the minimum validation loss, the largest θ_rel, then the largest λ (select_lambda_theta). A channel is “selected” if any of its edges survives.

2.6 Symbolic extraction, substitution and refit

Each surviving edge of the pruned model is fitted in three stages: a linear function, a library of affine-wrapped elementary functions, and PySR symbolic
regression (Cranmer, 2023) (60 s per edge; only edges carrying at least 5% of their layer’s score, at most 10 per model). A formula is accepted if its
validation R² exceeds 0.99. Accepted formulas replace their edges with trainable affine parameters. The registered procedure then refits all parameters,
which we did with unconstrained L-BFGS.

Methodological finding. In the simulation (Section 3.6) the substituted model without refit reproduced the pruned model’s shapes, whereas the
unconstrained refit drifted far from them, and in a few fits a formula left its domain (for example the logarithm of a negative argument) and produced
non-finite risks. The owner therefore fixed, before the real-data study, that the primary symbolic model is the substituted model without refit; the refitted
model is reported as secondary (D128). The real data confirmed the pattern (Section 4.3). Phase 2 tested a constrained refit (Section 5.2).

2.7 Metrics and statistical analysis

        Shape. Relative integrated squared error (RISE) of the centred effect against the centred truth, weighted by the empirical density of (X(t), t) in the
        test data. Because some directions of φ cannot affect any subject’s η (for example a component linear in x when ∫X dt is nearly constant across
        subjects), the primary metric is the identifiable RISE: error and truth are projected orthogonally to the directions of a 10 × 10 tensor B-spline
        space whose functional has relative variance below 3e-8 on the test curves. The time-homogeneous estimate of B2-H against the homogeneous
        truth uses a one-dimensional RISE. The primary shape summary is the mean over the two active channels.
        Survival. Survival-curve error against the simulation oracle; integrated Brier score (IBS) with inverse probability of censoring weights (Graf et al.,
        1999) (marginal, and conditional on z on real data); Harrell’s C (Harrell et al., 1982); Uno’s C (Uno et al., 2011) (τ the 90% quantile); D-calibration p
        (Haider et al., 2020). For B3: Brier score at the horizon, C within the horizon, and time-dependent AUC only when at least 10 cases and 10 controls
        exist.
        Selection. Recall of the active channels and false discovery rate (the null channel selected).
        Inference. Simulation: paired over replicates (mean difference, 95% t-interval, paired t, exact Wilcoxon, sign counts); equivalence by two one-
        sided tests (TOST) (Schuirmann, 1987). Real data: 5 outer splits by subject with the Nadeau–Bengio corrected resampled t-interval (Nadeau &
        Bengio, 2003). In Phase 1 only H1 and H-R12 are confirmatory; everything else is exploratory without multiplicity correction. Phase 2 added four
        confirmatory hypotheses (Section 5.1).
        Interpretability (real data). Stability: mean pairwise R² (squared cosine, so sign- and scale-invariant) and mean pairwise cosine of the centred
        time-averaged effects over 5 splits × 20 bootstrap resamples, on a common 50-point grid between the 5th and 95th percentiles. Clinical alignment:
        an effect is aligned if it is monotone in the pre-stated direction in at least 80% of these fits.

2.8 Pre-registration and software verification

Every round was registered in a decision log before its seeds were used, and every run, including failures, is reported. Twelve acceptance tests (CK-1 to
CK-12) with fixed thresholds and seeds were written before the simulation; failures were recorded and never converted by changing a seed or threshold.
Five failed at first and led to recorded owner decisions (repaired simulator and shape metric, convergence-based CoxKAN check, channel-level pruning
score, a stronger misspecification check), after which all but the AFCM check passed. The test suite at the end of Round 18:

3. Simulation study

3.1 Design

The simulator (DGP v2) generates n = 1,000 subjects per replicate with three channels on t ∈ [0, 1]: a random level, a random linear trend and four
Fourier modes per channel, observed with Gaussian noise at 40 dense times, or at 3–8 random visits in the sparse scenario. Channel 3 is a null channel.
Train/validation/test splits are 60/20/20, and censoring is about 30%. Each scenario has 20 replicates on fresh seeds (S-Add 3000–3019, S-Int 3100–3119,
S-Sparse 3200–3219, S-Misspec 3300–3319, S-Int/P0 3400–3419).

        S-Add: η = ∫sin(πX₁(t)/2)dt + ∫tanh(X₂(t))(1 + t)dt + 0.3z₁ − 0.3z₂, Weibull proportional hazards (shape 1.5), so the Cox model is correctly
        specified. φ₁ is time-homogeneous, φ₂ time-varying.
        S-Int: S-Add’s η plus 0.8 times the product of the two channels’ functional summaries (a cross-channel interaction that no additive model can
        represent).
        S-Sparse: S-Add with 3–8 visits per subject; B-spline smoothing against PACE.
        S-Misspec: S-Add’s η as an AFT location, log T = 1 − η/1.5 + 0.5ε with log-normal or log-logistic ε (non-PH; the Cox model is misspecified).
        S-Int/P0: the Round-1 simulator setting P0, re-testing KAN-FAE against MLP-FAE under strategy S3.

The study produced 1243 model records; 3 pruning/symbolic cells failed on a non-finite refit, were rerun after an evaluation-only harness fix, and are
reported with their original failed records.

The pre-registered rule declares “better” if the 95% CI lies below 0, “worse” if above, “equivalent” if within ±0.05 (TOST), and otherwise “inconclusive”.
H-R12 is inconclusive. The comparator failed its acceptance check (Section 2.4), so even a clear result would have compared B2-S with an unvalidated
AFCM. Against the earlier AFCM V0, B2-S was clearly better; V0 and V3 differ only in their penalty specification, so AFCM’s shape recovery depends
strongly on it. The time-varying effect φ₂ was recovered equivalently by both (TOST p 0.00064). Without the ensemble, single-seed B2-S had a higher
mean RISE (0.2073).

Pruning kept the active channels (recall 0.95 on S-Add) but did not reliably remove the null channel (FDR 0.13). About two thirds of the active edges
received an accepted formula. Substitution left the RISE essentially unchanged in both scenarios; the refit of all parameters by unconstrained L-BFGS
multiplied it several-fold, and 2 (S-Add) and 1 (S-Sparse) refits became non-finite. A plausible explanation (not tested separately) is that the refit has no
constraint keeping each substituted formula near the edge it approximated, so the formulas’ affine parameters can move their arguments outside the
domain of functions such as the logarithm.

training). With tuned reconstruction pre-training (S3) the survival gap vanished in Round 9 (F1) at the price of worse reconstruction, and the pre-
registered Round-12 re-test on 20 fresh seeds declared KAN and MLP equivalent within ±0.005 in curve error (90% CI [−0.0032, +0.0023]). In no arm,
strategy or setting was KAN-FAE found better than MLP-FAE on survival. Its interpretability was also limited:

Pruning removed almost nothing (Round 8 attributed this to BatchNorm making every encoder input unit-scale, so that no edge is small), and the
regularised variant lost reconstruction quality. Symbolic formulas were accepted for many encoder edges without loss of accuracy, but each maps one
abstract front-end feature to one latent unit, and the risk then passes through a further head; no formula for risk in terms of a clinical trajectory results.
The direct models of Sections 2–4 place the KAN edge on the trajectory itself.


4. Real-data applications

4.1 Data and cohorts

        PBC (pbcseq, R package survival (Therneau et al., 2026; Therneau & Grambsch, 2000; Murtaugh et al., 1994; Fleming & Harrington, 1991)): six
        laboratory channels (log bilirubin, albumin, log alkaline phosphatase, log AST, platelets, log prothrombin time), age and sex; single landmark at 730
        days with the whole history; endpoint E2 death or transplantation (primary) and E1 death (sensitivity).
        prothro (R package JM (Rizopoulos, 2010; Andersen et al., 1993)): prothrombin index; prednisone versus placebo; landmark 1 year.
        aids (JM (Rizopoulos, 2010; Guo & Carlin, 2004)): CD4; drug, sex, previous opportunistic infection, AZT failure; landmark 6 months.
        C-MAPSS FD001 (Saxena & Goebel, 2008; Saxena et al., 2008): turbofan run-to-failure sensor windows (Option B), a secondary data set used for
        the calibration question only.

Data-hygiene disclosures. The aids CD4 values are already on the square-root scale (non-integer values, maximum 24.1), although the package
documentation calls them counts, so they were used as provided. aids has 1,405 rows, not the 1,408 its documentation states. prothro has 488 patients;
its documentation gives both 488 and 467.

The leading B2-S effects were stable (time-averaged R² 0.986 for bilirubin, 0.966 for albumin, 0.985 for CD4) and aligned with the pre-stated clinical
directions. The exception was the prothrombin index under B2-S, monotone in the stated direction in only 72% of fits (threshold 80%), while B1-FPCA-1
aligned there (0.98). For B1-FPCA-1 every R² equals 1: its time-averaged effect is proportional to a single fixed function of x, and R² ignores sign and scale,
so the cosine (which can be low when the sign flips between fits) is the informative measure there. The weaker PBC markers had less stable B2-S effects
(AST: R² 0.64, cosine 0.12: the sign of the effect varied between fits), consistent with their rare selection.

5. Phase 2: pre-registered methodological revisions (Rounds 15–20)

5.1 Motivation and design

Phase 1 left three open problems: the refit after symbolic substitution was unusable (Section 3.6), so the symbolic model could only be used without refit;
on the real data the last observed value appeared to carry most of the information (Section 4.2); and the AFCM comparator was not validated (Section
2.4). Four further rounds tested targeted revisions prospectively. Each was registered in the decision log before its seeds were used, after a development
dry run on other seeds: Round 15 on S-Add 3500–3519, S-Sparse 3600–3619 and S-Last 3700–3719, Round 16 on S-Add 3800–3819, S-Sparse 3900–3919
and S-Last 4000–4019, and Round 17 on S-Last 4100–4119, S-Sparse 4200–4219 and S-Misspec-lognormal 4300–4319, and Round 18 on S-Last 4400–
4419, S-Sparse 4500–4519 and S-Misspec-lognormal 4600–4619, and Round 20 on S-Last 4700–4719, S-Sparse 4800–4819 and S-Misspec-lognormal
4900–4919. The simulator, sample size, splits, front end and ensembles were those of Section 3.

      Domain guard. A substituted formula containing log, sqrt or 1/x is evaluated with a smooth floor at half the smallest argument seen in training,
      and exp with a smooth cap 10 above the training range, so a formula cannot leave its domain during a refit.
      Functional distillation refit. The refit minimises the Cox loss plus μ times the variance-normalised squared distance between the substituted
      model and the pruned model it summarises (the B2 surfaces at every training subject and grid time, and the static edge activations), so the
      formulas’ parameters can adapt without drifting from the shapes they approximate. Round 15 chose μ ∈ {1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10} by validation partial
      likelihood. Round 16 fixed μ = 10, rejected a library candidate whose inner argument |a x + b| exceeds 50 anywhere on the edge’s training range,
      and made the refit safe: if it leaves a parameter or the objective non-finite, or does not lower the objective, every parameter is restored to its
      substituted value (a “fallback”, which is recorded). Each refit used 200 L-BFGS iterations.
      A landmark-anchored functional model (b2s_anchor_cox). η = Σ_d ψ_d(X_d(t_L)) + Σ_d ∫φ_d(X_d(t), t)dt + Σ_k ψ_k(z_k): a static KAN edge on
      each channel’s last observed value plus a gated B2-S term on the whole curve. The gate prunes functional channels by their integrated effect over
      the θ_rel grid of Section 2.5 and also offers “all off” (the model then reduces to a static CoxKAN on the last values). Round 15 chose among these
      settings with the parsimonious rule of Section 2.5 (tolerance 0.01), under which “all off” wins whenever it is within the tolerance; Round 16’s non-
      cliff rule applies the same rule only among settings that keep a channel, and takes “all off” only if its validation loss is strictly lower than the best of
      them. A residual variant (b2s_res_cox; the curve term acts on X(t) − X(t_L)) was a registered secondary in Round 15.
      Two-way gate (Round 17). The gate also prunes the last-value edges (“joint” states: both branches pruned at the same θ_rel; “static” states:
      every trajectory channel off) and keeps the plain B2-S model, fitted on the same split, as a candidate. The joint and static states are compared as in
      Round 16 (non-cliff); the chosen anchored state is used only if its validation loss is below the B2-S model’s by more than a tolerance last_tol, and
      otherwise the model is the B2-S model itself.
      Full-validation refit (Round 19, development check only). The Round-18 decision is kept; if anchoring is not confirmed the model is B2-S
      trained on the whole validation set, and if it is confirmed the chosen masks are refitted on the whole validation set.
      Confirmation split (Round 18). Each replicate’s validation subjects are split in half, stratified on the event, into val_select and val_confirm.
      Everything before the final decision uses val_select only, for both the anchored model and the B2-S comparator: tuning, early stopping, the
      candidate fine-tunes and the choice of the anchored state. The decision itself compares the chosen anchored candidate with the comparator’s first
      ensemble member on val_confirm, one model against one; anchoring is used only if it wins there by more than a margin, and otherwise the model
      is the comparator.
      A semiparametric functional KAN-AFT (NP-KAN-AFT, Round 20). log T = μ + η + ε with η the B2-S location and the law of ε left unspecified:
      it is the Kaplan–Meier estimate of the training residuals, so the predicted survival is S(t | Z) = S_KM(log t − η(Z)). Two objectives were compared in
      development: a Buckley–James residual EM (the Kaplan–Meier law re-estimated before every epoch and censored responses replaced by their
      conditional means) and a smoothed Gehan rank loss (Jose et al., 2025). This is the semiparametric AFT model with a functional KAN location; a
      Buckley–James KAN-AFT for static covariates is published, so it is not a new model class.
      Two-half cross-confirmation (Round 20). The Round-18 decision is made in both directions: select on val_select and confirm on val_confirm,
      and the reverse. In each direction the anchored ensemble (all three seeds) and the B2-S ensemble of the selecting half are compared by their mean
      member loss on the other half; anchoring is used only if it wins by more than a margin in both directions (relative to the loss for NP-KAN-AFT), and is
      then fine-tuned once more on the whole validation set; otherwise the model is B2-S trained on the whole validation set.
      A log-normal KAN-AFT (Round 17). log T = μ + η + σε with ε standard normal, for the comparator (B2-S AFT) and the anchored model, with the
      same two-way gate and the Round-16 distillation refit (Section 2.2 used a Weibull AFT).
      A last-value scenario (S-Last). η = sin(πX₁(1)/2) + 1.5 tanh(X₂(1)) + 0.3z₁ − 0.3z₂ with 3–8 visits: the risk depends only on the channels’ values
      at the end of the window, so a static model on the last values is close to correctly specified.

Hypotheses. H-R15a (Round 15) and H-R16a (Round 16), on S-Add and S-Sparse: all 40 distillation refits finite, and the S-Add mean difference in
identifiable RISE (distilled minus after pruning, paired over replicates) has an upper 95% bound below +0.05. H-R15b and H-R16b: on S-Last the survival-
curve error of the anchored model minus B2-S Cox has a 95% CI entirely below 0, and on S-Sparse the same difference has an upper 95% bound below
+0.005 (the anchored model may not lose to B2-S Cox where the trajectory matters). H-R17a repeats this test for the two-way gate. H-R17b, for the log-
normal KAN-AFT: all 20 distillation refits on S-Misspec finite with the same RISE bound, and for the two-way AFT model an upper bound below +0.005 on
S-Misspec and a 95% CI entirely below 0 on S-Last. H-R18a and H-R18b repeat the Cox and the AFT anchoring tests with the confirmation-split gate. H-
R20a: on S-Misspec the survival-curve error of NP-KAN-AFT minus B2-S Cox, and minus a B2-S Weibull KAN-AFT, each has an upper 95% bound below 0. H-
R20b: for Cox, the log-normal KAN-AFT and NP-KAN-AFT alike, the cross-confirmed model minus B2-S trained on the whole validation set has an upper
bound below 0 on S-Last and below the registered +0.005 on the trajectory scenario (S-Sparse for Cox, S-Misspec for the AFT models). All parts of a
hypothesis must hold. Everything else is exploratory.

In Round 15 distillation did what the unconstrained refit could not: it kept the substituted model close to the pruned shapes (S-Add RISE 0.262 against
1.202 after the old refit) and lowered the validation loss slightly. H-R15a nevertheless failed on both parts. One S-Add replicate (seed 3515) became non-
finite at every μ: an accepted library formula on a baseline-covariate edge was nearly degenerate (a softplus with a very steep inner argument and a tiny
output scale), and the first L-BFGS step sent the parameters to overflow, a numerical failure the domain guard cannot prevent. And validation selection
often chose a loose anchor: at a fixed μ = 10 the S-Add RISE change was −0.0008 ([−0.0018, +0.0002]), whereas the replicates in which validation chose
μ = 0.1 changed by +0.033 on average. These post-hoc observations motivated Round 16’s three changes, which were then tested on fresh seeds.

In Round 16 all 40 distillation refits were finite and the fallback was never needed; the bound on |a x + b| rejected 2 (S-Add) and 1 (S-Sparse) previously
accepted formulas. At μ = 10 the distilled model reproduced the pruned shapes (S-Add RISE difference −0.0004, [−0.0013, +0.0006]), so H-R16a is
supported. The anchor that makes the refit safe also makes it nearly inert: relative to the substituted model without refit, neither the survival-curve error
([−0.0004, +0.0001] on S-Add) nor the validation loss ([−0.0003, +0.0007]) changed. The result therefore shows that a refit, if one is wanted, can be
made safe by anchoring it strongly; it does not show that a refit adds anything to substitution alone.

In Round 15 the anchored model was clearly better than B2-S Cox on S-Last ([−0.0222, −0.0149]) and better than landmark Cox on both scenarios, but
on S-Sparse its upper bound (+0.0094) exceeded the margin. The loss came from replicates in which the gate switched every functional channel off (4 of
20; mean difference +0.0184 there, against +0.0012 where it kept a channel): a “cliff” at which the parsimonious rule preferred the simplest model
although the trajectory carried signal. The residual variant was worse than B2-S Cox on S-Sparse (+0.0149): a nonlinear effect of X(t) is not the sum of an
effect of X(t_L) and one of X(t) − X(t_L). Before Round 16 used any seed, the non-cliff rule was applied to the saved Round-15 gate grids: it would have
reduced the S-Sparse replicates with every channel off only from 4 to 3, because in the others “all off” was strictly better on the validation data, so a
repeat failure of the second part was anticipated and recorded (D138, D139).

In Round 16 the S-Last part held again ([−0.0212, −0.0140]), and the non-cliff rule kept trajectory channels more often on S-Last (every channel off in 15
replicates, against 19 under the D133 rule) without changing the curve error. On S-Sparse, however, both rules switched every channel off in only 1
replicate and made identical decisions, and the anchored model was still slightly worse than B2-S Cox (+0.0032, [+0.0011, +0.0053]; worse in 17 of 20
replicates), so H-R16b is not supported. The anticipated mechanism was therefore wrong: post hoc, the loss was +0.0024 ([+0.0010, +0.0038]) in the
19 replicates in which the gate kept a channel. Adding static last-value edges costs a little accuracy when the effect runs through the whole trajectory and
gains much more when the risk is carried by the last value (S-Last); a gate on the trajectory term cannot remove that cost, which would require gating the
last-value edges as well (not tested).

5.4 Two-way gated anchoring and a log-normal KAN-AFT (H-R17a, H-R17b)

Round 17 asked whether the small cost of anchoring on S-Sparse disappears if the last-value edges are gated as well, and whether the Phase-2 tools carry
over to a KAN-AFT. The two-way gate (Section 5.1) can fall back to the plain B2-S model itself, so a replicate in which anchoring is not chosen contributes
a difference of exactly 0. The tolerance last_tol was chosen by a rule fixed before the development runs, on already-used Round-16 seeds for Cox (0.01)
and on those seeds plus development seeds for the log-normal AFT (0.04, the largest value of the grid); the registration was locked afterwards (D141).

On the development seeds the Cox two-way model removed most of the Round-16 penalty on S-Sparse (+0.0003, [−0.0007, +0.0013]). On fresh seeds it

anchor is biased toward anchoring; an independent confirmation split, or comparing equally selected candidates, would remove that bias.

For the log-normal KAN-AFT, H-R17b is supported. All 20 distillation refits were finite and reproduced the pruned shapes ([−0.0011, +0.0000]), where
the unanchored refit raised the mean RISE to 0.452 from 0.099; as for Cox, the distilled model did not predict better than the substituted one. The two-
way AFT model did not lose on the trajectory-driven S-Misspec data ([−0.0008, +0.0023]) and improved on S-Last ([−0.0095, −0.0023]). Its strict
tolerance made it conservative: it fell back to B2-S AFT in 12 of the S-Last replicates, kept about a third of the gain of the anchored alternative (−0.0177),
and remained worse than landmark Cox there (+0.0059). The success of H-R17b thus rests on a gate that anchors cautiously: the same trade-off as for
Cox, resolved in favour of not losing.

5.5 Anchoring decided on a confirmation split (H-R18a, H-R18b)

In Round 17 the anchored state was the best of many fine-tuned candidates on the validation data, and the same validation data then decided whether it
beat the single B2-S model. Round 18 tested whether deciding on held-out subjects removes that optimism (Section 5.1). The development check on the
already-used Round-17 seeds showed the expected pattern (gaps are comparator minus anchored loss, so positive favours anchoring): on S-Sparse the
chosen anchored state looked better than B2-S Cox on val_select (+0.0171 in mean loss) but worse on val_confirm (−0.0115), while on S-Last its
advantage held up (+0.0704 and +0.0576). A zero margin still left the Cox S-Sparse bound at +0.0053, and the rule fixed before the development runs
chose a margin of 0.02 for Cox and 0.02 for the AFT model, the largest value of the grid in both cases.

On fresh seeds both hypotheses were supported. For Cox the gate anchored in 15 of 20 S-Last replicates and kept a clear gain ([−0.0187, −0.0090]); on
S-Sparse it anchored in 7, tied B2-S Cox exactly in 13 and stayed within the margin ([−0.0057, +0.0028]): H-R18a is supported. For the log-normal AFT
model the gate almost never anchored on S-Misspec (1 of 20; [−0.0002, +0.0004]) but anchored in 12 S-Last replicates, more than the Round-17 gate,
with a larger gain ([−0.0151, −0.0056]): H-R18b is supported.

Two qualifications matter. First, the registered comparator is itself trained on half the usual validation data. Against B2-S Cox trained as in earlier rounds
on the whole validation set, the confirmation-gated model remained better on S-Last ([−0.0205, −0.0094]) but its S-Sparse bound was +0.0093, which
would not meet the margin; the cost of setting val_confirm aside falls on the comparator as much as on the anchored model. Second, the margins were
tuned in-sample and lie at the edge of their grid. The optimism diagnostic did not repeat cleanly on the formal Cox S-Sparse seeds (mean advantage
+0.0114 on val_select and +0.0105 on val_confirm), so the evidence that selection optimism alone caused Round 17’s failure is mixed.

5.6 Refitting on the whole validation set (development check)

Round 18’s estimators were compared with a B2-S model trained on half of the validation data. Round 19 asked whether the confirmation decision still
holds up against the usual B2-S trained on the whole validation set, if the anchored model is refitted on the whole validation set once anchoring is
confirmed and the full-validation B2-S is used otherwise (Section 5.1). The design, two refit variants, a margin rule and a go/no-go rule were fixed before a
development check on the already-used Round-18 seeds. The check failed its go/no-go rule, so no formal test was run: H-R19a and H-R19b are
untested, and their fresh seeds remain unused (D147, D148).

5.7 Semiparametric KAN-AFT and cross-confirmation (H-R20a, H-R20b)

Two questions remained. Every AFT model so far fixed the error distribution (Weibull in Section 2.2, log-normal in Round 17), so its survival curves are
biased whenever the family is wrong, however well the location is learned. And the Round-18 confirmation compared the anchored candidate with a single
B2-S member trained on half the validation data, in one direction only; against B2-S trained on the whole validation set it did not keep Cox within the S-
Sparse margin (Section 5.6). Round 20 tested NP-KAN-AFT and the two-half cross-confirmation (Section 5.1). Two development stages on the already-used
Round-18 seeds fixed the NP-KAN-AFT objective and the margins by rules set before the runs, and the hypotheses were then tested on fresh seeds (D150,
D151).

Development. The smoothed Gehan objective had the lower average curve error over S-Sparse and S-Misspec (0.0598 against 0.0609 for Buckley–
James) and was chosen (Table 34). The margin rule chose 0.02 for Cox, its fall-back and the largest value of the grid, and 0 for both AFT models (Table
35); both go rules passed.

(−0.0054 and −0.0084). Refitting without the confirmation step would have cost on every trajectory scenario (Table 39), so the confirmation, not the refit,
carries the non-inferiority.

5.9 AFCM smoothing by Laplace marginal likelihood (development check)

To repair the comparator, smoothing parameters were chosen by a Laplace approximate marginal likelihood (LAML, with the Breslow observed
information) instead of validation loss. The registered pass rule (D134) required the CK-6c criterion, φ₁ below 0.15 and φ₂ below 0.10, on all three seeds
22, 914, 966 before seed 24 would be used.

6. Discussion

6.1 Principal findings

     1. Direct functional KANs are a workable parametrisation of the additive functional Cox model, not a better one. B2-S and AFCM V3
        recovered the S-Add shapes to a similar degree and could not be separated by the confirmatory test; both were far better than linear-in-scores two-
        stage models when the effect is nonlinear.
     2. Interpretability tools work when used conservatively. Channel-level pruning found the active channels (with imperfect removal of the null
        one); symbolic formulas substituted without refit reproduced the model; leading real-data effects were stable and pointed in clinically expected
        directions. An unconstrained refit after substitution should be avoided; a refit anchored to the pruned model at a fixed weight, with a fallback and a
        bound on formula arguments, was safe in every replicate (H-R16a) but did not improve prediction.
     3. No predictive advantage on small real cohorts. Simple landmark models were at least as good; with so few visits per subject, the last
        observed value plausibly carried most of the information (an interpretation, not a tested finding).
     4. KAN blocks inside an autoencoder did not help. KAN-FAE was worse than or equivalent to MLP-FAE in every comparison, and its edges were
        not readable as clinical effects.
     5. Anchoring to the last observed value is a trade-off, not a free gain. The anchored model was better than B2-S Cox and landmark Cox when
        risk depended on the last values, and slightly worse than B2-S Cox when it depended on the trajectory, in Rounds 15 and 16. Neither the non-cliff
        rule nor a two-way gate that could fall back to B2-S (Round 17) removed the cost reliably on fresh seeds; deciding on a held-out confirmation split
        with a margin (Round 18) kept most of the gain and stayed within the registered margin, against a comparator that also used only half of the
        validation data; against B2-S trained on the whole validation set, refitting the anchored model did not keep Cox within the S-Sparse margin (Round
        19, development check). Confirming the decision in both halves of the validation split against three-seed B2-S ensembles did keep Cox, the log-
        normal KAN-AFT and NP-KAN-AFT within the margin against that comparator on fresh seeds (Round 20), mainly by anchoring less often.
     6. The Phase-2 tools carry over to KAN-AFT. For a log-normal KAN-AFT the anchored distillation refit was finite in every replicate and preserved
        the shapes (H-R17b part 1), as for Cox.
     7. The AFT error law need not be chosen. A semiparametric KAN-AFT, whose error law is the Kaplan–Meier estimate of the residuals, was better
        than Cox and Weibull models under log-normal errors and as good as the correctly specified log-normal model (H-R20a); it is the classical
        semiparametric AFT model with a functional KAN location.

6.2 Relation to prior work

Our results are consistent with the view that the additive functional Cox model (Cui et al., 2021) already captures the model form a single-layer functional
CoxKAN offers. What KAN parametrisation adds is a uniform toolkit of pruning and symbolic summaries and the option to compose layers; in our
interaction scenario the composed B2-deep did not use that option to advantage. KAN survival models with static covariates (Knottenbelt et al., 2025;
Jose et al., 2025; Mastroleo et al., 2026; Boulitsakis Logothetis et al., 2026) and the KAN joint model abstract (Lundin et al., 2025) address different input
structures, and we make no claim relative to work we could read only in abstract.

6.3 Limitations

       Unvalidated comparator. AFCM V3 failed its single-fit acceptance check; its shape recovery depends on how the validation-chosen penalties fall
       on a given data set (one λ_t shared by a time-homogeneous and a time-varying channel trades one against the other). AFCM is a Python re-
       implementation without REML; Laplace marginal-likelihood selection did not repair it (Section 5.9).
       Phase 2 was motivated post hoc. The Round-15 to Round-17 revisions were designed after looking at earlier rounds’ failures (on other seeds),
       tested on one simulator, and the Round-16 and Round-17 changes were not run on real data; the Round-15 real-data analyses used the same data
       that motivated the anchored design.
       Tolerances tuned on few seeds. Round 17’s last_tol values were chosen on the already-used Round-16 replicates (and development seeds for S-
       Misspec); the Cox value did not transfer to fresh seeds (H-R17a), and the AFT value lies at the edge of its grid. Round 18’s margins were also tuned
       in-sample and also lie at the edge of the grid.
       The confirmation split halves the validation data. Round 18’s comparator was trained on val_select; against the usual full-validation B2-S Cox,
       the S-Sparse non-inferiority of the confirmation-gated model was not shown, and the Round-19 refit did not change that in development (H-R19a
       and H-R19b were not tested). Round 20’s cross-confirmation met the margin against the full-validation comparator on fresh seeds.
       Round-20 settings chosen on reused seeds. The NP-KAN-AFT objective and the margins were chosen on development seeds used for the third
       time, and the Cox margin lies at the edge of its grid. The Round-19 miss and the Round-20 pass are on different seeds, so the cross-confirmation is
       supported by a fresh-seed test but not shown to be the cause of the improvement; the conservative Cox margin also gave up part of the S-Last
       gain.
       NP-KAN-AFT was tested under one error law. Its advantage over the Cox and Weibull models reflects their misspecification under log-normal
       errors; it was not better than the correct parametric family, and its predicted survival does not extrapolate beyond the largest training residual.
       One simulator, 20 replicates. H-R12 rests on one DGP with three channels and n = 1,000.
       Small real-data cohorts with few visits, so all intervals are wide; five outer splits give limited resolution.
       PACE failed on one PBC split (non-finite curves on a gappy visit design); the PACE sensitivity row has 4 PBC E2 splits.
       Coarse clinical alignment. Monotonicity over the 5th–95th percentiles is a crude check; clinical sign-off is external, as is the choice of the PBC
       endpoint.
       No joint model or deep dynamic model (JM, Dynamic-DeepHit) was fitted; the two-stage mixed-effects Cox model stands in for the joint-model
       class.
      Framing (b) is conditional on configurations selected and gated for the MLP; it shows that the KAN encoder did not help under these
      configurations, not that it cannot.
      Targeted literature review. No systematic review was done, so no novelty claim is made.

6.4 Reproducibility

All code, decision logs, pre-registrations, raw records and this manuscript are in one repository. Public data were obtained from CRAN (survival 3.8-12, JM
1.5-2) and NASA’s prognostics repository, with checksums in the run manifest. Each round’s plan was committed before its seeds were used. Every
number in this manuscript is rendered from the saved records, logged with its source, and re-checked by an independent script and a unit test (Appendix
A).


7. Conclusions

Functional CoxKAN and KAN-AFT models that apply KAN edges directly to longitudinal trajectories recover nonlinear functional effects, support channel
selection and give accurate symbolic summaries when the formulas are substituted without refitting. In our pre-registered comparisons they were not
better than the additive functional Cox model (whose re-implementation could not itself be validated) or than simple landmark baselines on small clinical
cohorts, and burying KAN blocks inside a functional autoencoder gave neither better prediction nor clinically readable effects. A second, pre-registered
phase made the symbolic refit safe (a strongly anchored, NaN-safe distillation refit), at the cost of making it nearly inert, and showed that anchoring a
functional model to the last observed values helps when the last value carries the risk and costs a little when the trajectory does; a two-way gate did not
remove that cost reliably for Cox, and a cautious gate for a log-normal KAN-AFT avoided it only by giving up most of the gain; deciding on a held-out
confirmation split met every registered criterion for both, at the price of halving the validation data available to each model, and against B2-S trained on
the whole validation set it could not be shown to avoid the S-Sparse cost for Cox. Confirming the decision in both halves of the validation split against
three-seed B2-S ensembles closed that gap on fresh seeds, for Cox and AFT models, by anchoring less often, and a semiparametric KAN-AFT with a
Kaplan–Meier error law performed as well as the correctly specified parametric model without having to know it. These negative, equivalence and trade-
off findings, with the full record behind them, are the contribution.

                                                                            non-inferiority; the Cox margin 0.02 makes the Cox gate
                                                                            conservative (9/20 confirmed on S-Last, against 14/20
                                                                            under the Round-18 one-direction rule at margin 0); on S-
                                                                            Last the Cox cross-confirmed model did not differ from
                                                                            landmark Cox (+0.0011 [−0.0036, +0.0058]) while the AFT
                                                                            families were better than landmark Cox (log-normal
                                                                            −0.0054 [−0.0094, −0.0014], NP −0.0084 [−0.0126,
                                                                            −0.0043]). Interpretation limits: one simulator; margins and
                                                                            the NP objective chosen on development seeds used three
                                                                            times; the Cox margin at the grid edge; the Round-19 miss
                                                                            and this pass are on different seeds, so the fix is supported
                                                                            by this test, not proven to be the cause.

Project instructions (the repository README.md is intentionally left unchanged, D28).
### environment (project-local; never touches the global Python)
bash scripts/setup_env.sh                          # or: KANFAE_FROM_LOCK=1 bash scripts/setup_env.sh
bash scripts/verify_env.sh                         # E-1 / E-5 evidence
### tests (every attempt is appended to reports/logs/test_records.jsonl)
KANFAE_RUN_ID=rerun .venv/bin/python -m pytest -v -rA tests/
### data (public sources; checksums in reports/run_manifest.json)
###   C-MAPSS: https://phm-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/NASA/6.+Turbofan+Engine+Degradation+Simulation+Data+Set.zip
###            -> extract inner CMAPSSData.zip into data/raw/cmapss/
###   PBC:     https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/survival_3.8-12.tar.gz -> data/raw/pbc/{DESCRIPTION,data/pbc.rda}
### experiments (resumable; completed run IDs are skipped)
bash scripts/run_all_experiments.sh                # synthetic (5 replicates x 6 settings) + C-MAPSS (5 splits)

Functional Kolmogorov–Arnold survival models for longitudinal covariates: pre-registered
comparisons, safer symbolic summaries and confirmed landmark anchoring

Manuscript draft, Round 19 (D147–D149; supersedes the Round-18 draft, which is kept unchanged, as are the Round-14, Round-16 and Round-17 drafts). Generated from saved records
by scripts/manuscript_round19.py; every number below is read from a record and logged with its source in reports/manuscript_values_round19.json (Appendix A). Draft for the
owner’s review: not peer reviewed; authors, affiliations, funding and competing interests to be completed by the owner.

Authors: [to be completed by the owner]
Status: draft manuscript of a pre-registered empirical study; no novelty claim (D111).


Abstract

Background. Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (KANs) replace the weights of a neural network by learnable univariate functions and have been adapted to
survival analysis with static covariates (Knottenbelt et al., 2025; Jose et al., 2025). Many clinical and engineering problems instead have covariates
measured repeatedly over time. A single-layer functional KAN under the Cox loss has the same model form as the additive functional Cox model (AFCM)
(Cui et al., 2021), so any contribution must be empirical.

Methods. We report a sequence of pre-registered studies. A motivating study (framing b) embedded KAN blocks in a functional autoencoder (KAN-FAE)
and compared it with a parameter-matched MLP autoencoder (MLP-FAE). The primary study (framing a) evaluated direct functional KAN survival models:
functional CoxKAN and functional KAN-AFT with time-homogeneous (B2-H), separable bivariate (B2-S) and two-layer (B2-deep) functional layers; two-
stage models on functional principal component scores or trajectory summaries (B1); and stacked landmark supermodels (B3). Comparators were a re-
implementation of AFCM, an FPCA Cox model, a two-stage mixed-effects Cox model, summary-based Cox and random survival forest models and a
landmark Cox model. A simulation study (four scenarios, 20 replicates each) had a single confirmatory test (H-R12): B2-S Cox minus AFCM in identifiable
shape error (RISE). Real-data analyses (PBC, two JM data sets, C-MAPSS) were exploratory. A second phase (Rounds 15–19) tested, on fresh simulation
seeds and with pre-registered multi-part criteria, a distillation refit for the symbolic summaries, a landmark-anchored functional model that adds the last
observed values to B2-S, a two-way gate that can fall back to B2-S, and both tools in a log-normal KAN-AFT.

Results. H-R12 was inconclusive: B2-S Cox minus AFCM V3 was +0.0065 (95% CI [−0.0506, +0.0635]; paired-t p 0.815; equivalence within ±0.05 not
shown, TOST p 0.0634), and the AFCM comparator failed its own single-fit acceptance check. Both direct functional models recovered nonlinear shapes far
better than a linear-in-scores FPCA model (B2-S minus B1-FPCA-1: −0.5566, better in 20 of 20 replicates). Substituting accepted symbolic formulas
preserved the learned shapes (S-Add RISE 0.214 before and 0.212 after substitution), whereas the customary unconstrained refit degraded them (1.604).
On the real data no functional or KAN model predicted clearly better than simple landmark baselines; every Nadeau–Bengio interval for the integrated
Brier score of B2-S Cox minus a baseline included 0. In Phase 2, a distillation refit with a fixed anchor weight, a NaN-safe fallback and a bound on formula
arguments kept all 40 refits finite and preserved the pruned shapes (H-R16a supported, S-Add RISE difference −0.0004; its validation-tuned predecessor
H-R15a had failed). A landmark-anchored model that adds the last observed values to B2-S was clearly better than B2-S Cox when risk depended on the
last values (S-Last, −0.0176) but slightly worse when it depended on the whole trajectory (S-Sparse, +0.0032), so H-R15b and H-R16b were not
supported. A two-way gate that falls back to B2-S unless anchoring wins on validation kept the S-Last gain but again missed the S-Sparse margin on fresh
seeds (upper bound +0.0053; H-R17a not supported), while for a log-normal KAN-AFT the distillation refit and a more conservative two-way gate met
every registered criterion (H-R17b supported). Deciding on held-out validation subjects whether to anchor (Round 18) met every registered criterion for
Cox and for the AFT model (H-R18a and H-R18b supported; S-Sparse bound for Cox +0.0028), although against B2-S trained on the whole validation set
the S-Sparse bound was wider; refitting the anchored model on the whole validation set did not close that gap in a development check, so no formal test
was run (Round 19). Pruning selected a stable, clinically plausible set of PBC markers, and the leading effects were stable over 100 bootstrap fits and
aligned with the pre-stated clinical directions, with one exception (prothrombin index under B2-S). In the motivating study, KAN-FAE had higher survival-
curve error than MLP-FAE in the confirmatory test (H1: +0.0078, p 0.047), the two were equivalent under reconstruction pre-training on fresh seeds
(−0.0005, TOST p 0.0049), and the autoencoder’s KAN edges acted on abstract features rather than on clinical trajectories.

Conclusions. Direct functional KAN survival models are a workable, interpretable parametrisation of the additive functional Cox model, with usable
pruning and symbolic summaries when the formulas are substituted without refitting. We found no evidence of a predictive advantage over established
methods, and placing KAN blocks inside a functional autoencoder gave neither better prediction nor readable effects. A strongly anchored refit makes the
symbolic summaries safe to refit but does not improve on substitution alone, for Cox and AFT models alike; anchoring to the last observed values helps
when they carry the risk and is hard to switch off reliably when they do not. All findings beyond the registered hypotheses (H1, H-R12, H-R15a/b, H-
R16a/b, H-R17a/b, H-R18a/b) are exploratory.


Keywords

Kolmogorov–Arnold networks; functional data; survival analysis; additive functional Cox model; landmarking; pre-registration; equivalence testing;
negative results; symbolic regression; interpretability.


1. Introduction

1.1 Functional covariates in survival analysis

Repeated measurements of a biomarker or a sensor are naturally viewed as a curve X(t) observed with noise at a few times (Ramsay & Silverman, 2005).
The linear functional Cox model enters the curve through ∫β(t)X(t)dt (Gellar et al., 2015; Kong et al., 2018), and its coefficient can also vary with follow-up
time (Du & Leroux, 2024). The additive functional Cox model (AFCM) of Cui et al. (2021) replaces the linear term by ∫F(X(s), s)ds with a bivariate smooth
F, following functional generalised additive models (McLean et al., 2014); it is estimated with penalised tensor-product splines. Sparse, irregular visits are
commonly handled by principal components analysis through conditional expectation (PACE) (Yao et al., 2005). Dynamic prediction uses joint models
(Wulfsohn & Tsiatis, 1997; Tsiatis & Davidian, 2004; Rizopoulos, 2010), landmarking and landmark supermodels (van Houwelingen, 2007; van
Houwelingen & Putter, 2012; Putter & van Houwelingen, 2022), or deep models of the covariate history (Lee et al., 2020; Hu & Nan, 2025; Gao et al.,
2025).

Neural Cox models such as DeepSurv (Katzman et al., 2018) gain flexibility at the cost of readable effects. KANs (Liu et al., 2025) place a learnable
univariate function on every edge, which makes each edge a candidate for visualisation, pruning and symbolic regression. CoxKAN (Knottenbelt et al.,
2025), KAN-AFT (Jose et al., 2025), SurvKAN (Mastroleo et al., 2026) and KAPLAN (Boulitsakis Logothetis et al., 2026) all use static covariates; their time-
varying elements concern effects that change with follow-up time, not covariates measured over time. A KAN joint model with yearly landmarks was
found only as a conference abstract (Lundin et al., 2025), and F-KAN feeds functional principal component scores to a KAN for a scalar response (Qin & Li,
2026).

1.2 Architectural motivation: KAN blocks inside a functional autoencoder

The project began (Rounds 1–9) with a different architecture: a functional autoencoder (Wu et al., 2024) whose encoder used KAN blocks, with an AFT
survival head on the latent representation (KAN-FAE), against a parameter-matched MLP encoder (MLP-FAE). The hope was that a KAN encoder would give
both better prediction and readable effects. Two findings ended that line (Section 3.7 gives the numbers).

   1. No predictive advantage. The conventional MLP-FAE first had to pass a pre-registered learnability gate; every design failed it until Round 8 (Table
      1 lists the gate looks with saved verdict records). Under the configuration that passed, the single confirmatory test (H1) found KAN-FAE worse than
      MLP-FAE in survival-curve error. With reconstruction pre-training (strategy S3) the two were indistinguishable, and a fresh-seed re-test in Round 12
      declared them equivalent within a pre-registered margin.
   2. No clinical readability. In an autoencoder the KAN edges act on abstract front-end features and feed latent units that a further head combines
      into risk. Pruning removed almost no edge, and the symbolic formulas, though accurate, described maps between abstract coordinates rather than
      effects of a clinical variable.

These results motivated the direct design studied in the rest of this paper: put the KAN where the clinical variable enters, ∫φ(X(t), t)dt, so that each
learned function is an effect of a measured trajectory.
